title: The Best Educational Reform We’re Completely Ignoring
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Teacher Kevin Stinehart argues that the most powerful school reform available is the one schools keep cutting: unstructured recess and play. He frames play as a developmental necessity and reads rising anxiety, frayed peer relationships and teacher burnout as possible symptoms of play deprivation rather than discipline problems. He cites his own high-poverty South Carolina school, where prioritizing play before, during and after school coincided with fewer behavior issues, higher test scores and a 100 percent parent approval rating. The bulk of the piece is parent testimony about his Play Club, followed by a list of what recess teaches and a cost argument. It ends with a call to advocate for play.
points: Recess is where children practice problem-solving, empathy, resilience and conflict negotiation, so treating it as a reward undermines learning itself.
Stinehart's school reports lower behavior issues and rising test scores after committing to unstructured play, offered as practical evidence of school culture change.
Parent testimonials describe gains in confidence, cooperation and friendship that carried over to home life.
Recess works as peer-directed social-emotional learning that needs no curriculum, app or budget line, only time, space and trust.
quotes: Children are wired to learn through movement, social interactions, and unstructured time. Play is where they practice problem-solving, develop empathy, build resilience, and negotiate conflict. It’s not a detour from the learning process. It is the process.

Look around most classrooms today and you’ll see the fallout of ignoring this truth: rising anxiety, frayed peer relationships, chronic stress, emotional dysregulation, and teacher burnout. We often chalk these issues up to behavior or discipline problems. But what if what we’re really seeing is actually play deprivation?

The results were undeniable. Behavior issues dropped dramatically. Standardized test scores rose significantly. Our school culture became healthier and more joyful. And in our high-poverty public school, we achieved something unprecedented: a 100% parent approval rating on South Carolina’s state report card.
These stories are not extraordinary. They’re everyday miracles made possible by a very simple gift: time to play with other kids.

Since the early 2000s, recess has been steadily reduced in schools across the U.S. in favor of more class time. It’s well-meaning, but counterproductive. Because what we’re losing isn’t just downtime. We’re losing the place kids grow, develop, and make their minds fertile soil for the academic goals we have for them.
Recess doesn’t require a curriculum. Or an app. Or a new position in the district budget. It requires time. Space. And trust.

We already spend millions trying to fix problems that recess naturally addresses. From classroom behavior to student anxiety, the evidence is overwhelming: kids don’t need more control. They need more freedom.
